utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld. Is there a matter you want to raise before we go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, there is. Very briefly, I believe at the close of business yesterday, the Court ordered that the statement be marked as an exhibit. I'm just wondering, in light of the fact that we did move into closed session for one very brief period, that -- I'm asking if the Court might either seal that exhibit and mark it confidential so that it doesn't go into the public domain, or it will have to be the subject of some redaction in order to ensure that the purpose of going into closed session is not obviated by the exhibit itself being a completely open document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will seal it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is one matter, Mr. Ryneveld, while you're on your feet. We've got a new list of 92 bis witnesses. I don't know if you're dealing with this aspect of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Part of the aspect of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let me point this out: That as I understand it, some of these witnesses have not yet been ruled on by the Chamber. We ruled, I think, on 23 witnesses, as I recollect. There's now 33 on the list which you propose to call. Not all have been specifically ruled on, I think I'm right in saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for bringing that to my attention. Perhaps during the break -- needless to say, we would be proposing to call those witnesses first that the Chamber has already ruled upon. Otherwise, we'd have to seek an oral application before they would be permitted to give evidence, but thank you for raising that with me; but so as to save time, after this witness has been -- has completed his evidence, we would propose to start the 92 bis proceedings and hopefully the ones we have lined up are ones that are part of the 23 that the Court has already approved. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the first in the original list, the first six were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But perhaps you could look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I will certainly during the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, at the end of your testimony, you explained how an officer gave you a map with precise indications of the places of attack of the Yugoslav forces on the KLA.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said an official gave me the information about how the Serbian forces would attack the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the map, you drew the exact spots and directions, the routes that you got from him, the axes that the forces of Yugoslavia used. That's what you claimed.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he pointed out to me on the map what later appeared to be and generally was the way the Serbian forces dealt with the KLA, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You marked the direction they took on the map. You indicated it and then marked it on the map.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I marked the general direction of the main body of the forces. Obviously, there were many more sort of battles going on around Kosovo, but the activity day-to-day by the Serbian forces followed generally that direction that I gave, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you claim that the map was shown to you by an official officer, are you conscious of the fact that if that were to have been correct and as there are facts in this connection that you are an officer of the enemy side who -- and which prior -- immediately prior to the attack on Yugoslavia, you were an officer, then -- and as the office -- if the officer gave you those facts, then he would have jeopardised the lives of his many comrades, members of the Yugoslav army. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first place, Mr. Milosevic, I wasn't aware that, as verifiers, we were your enemy while we were in Kosovo. We were actually working very closely with your forces, being completely impartial and certainly not behaving in any form as an enemy. Secondly, this official was, I believe, so fed up with the whole thing that he was prepared to give me an indication of what was going to happen, knowing that we were going to leave and there would be no internal possibility of anything being able to be done by, as you would say, the enemy forces from outside to your plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he gave it to you after a meeting at which you discussed the withdrawal of the mission. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had been discussing the withdrawal over several sessions, but by this point we had already indicated that we probably would be leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as everyone in Yugoslavia knew, not only the soldiers but the whole population knew that the mission was withdrawing to enable the start of the bombing, the NATO bombing, I assume you would have no doubt as to the fact that your interlocutor knew about this too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are two questions there, Colonel. The first question is this: Did the mission withdraw to enable the start of the bombing or the bombing to start. The second question is: Did the interlocutor know it? Perhaps you'd like to answer them separately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The first answer is: There was certainly no intention to withdraw because we were about to start bombing. The reason we withdrew, I already made clear in my evidence, was because (a) our job was becoming too dangerous from the activities of the MUP and the VJ towards us; secondly, the number of your forces had increased dramatically and, therefore, there was general fighting taking place. Access was, therefore, restricted. We couldn't go to the border. We basically couldn't do our work. And this is exactly the reason we gave for why we left Kosovo. For no other reason. And the second -- sorry. I apologise. Your second answer about the -- my interlocutor, whether he knew that we were leaving, he certainly knew but what he thought was going to happen next, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the whole planet knew that the mission had withdrawn so that it should not be subjected to NATO bombing or, rather, that the states which had representatives in the mission withdrew their men and the OSCE made a decision to that effect, that the people should be withdrawn, not to have to be exposed to the NATO bombing, which was completely imminent at that time. Is that so or is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's not. As I said, the only reason we withdrew -- we would have happily stayed for whatever time it required to conclude our mission. We left because we could not work. The subsequent action was not connected with our departure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However much you claim that it wasn't connected with your departure, you know full well that at the border towards Yugoslavia, especially in Macedonia, there was an amassment of NATO troops and everywhere - in the information media and everywhere else - the threat of bombing was voiced, and the Yugoslav forces stepped up the border belt, their presence in the border belt, and we sent reinforcements precisely because war was imminent, the threat of war that loomed over Yugoslavia. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are a number of assertions there. The first is that there was -- NATO troops were massing on the border towards Yugoslavia. Is that so or not, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We certainly had an extraction force sitting in Trnovo which was intended to help us pull out of Kosovo if our sort of extraction wasn't permitted by Belgrade. And yes, there were forces building up in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's get this right. And then the next point that's being made is that the threat of bombing was being voiced everywhere, in the information media and elsewhere. Can you assist us as to that? At the time was there that threat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the media in general were saying that -- words to that effect, that a war could start and that there was a threat of bombing, yes. I think that was quite clear in the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the final point that's made is that Yugoslav forces were being reinforced near the border. Again, is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Yugoslav forces were being reinforced throughout Kosovo. All the garrisons were being strengthened. Certainly all the border areas, the bridges, the tunnels were prepared for demolition, which is standard procedure if the country's under threat, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. So in fact, you confirm that Yugoslavia, at that point in time, was on a state of alert with war imminent. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think you can say that you were prepared for war, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we were faced with the danger of war in view of everything you said a moment ago, the build-up of forces in Macedonia and the generally known threat that the bombing would start. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was -- what you say is correct that there was a build-up of forces in Macedonia, and the media were speculating that there would be a bombing attack against possibly Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it only the media that was speculating or were there statements quite clear, crisp statements from the top officials of the western countries who said that an intervention would take place, as they called it, an intervention against our country?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in general, Mr. Milosevic, I can't answer this question because I don't really -- can't remember at the time what the press exactly were saying, which officials from which countries, what they were saying, but I think that I will go along with your story that there was speculation that there would be bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you can explain this away as being speculation, but I don't think there's a single western leader who did not make statements of that kind publicly. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is it logical that a country, which is being threatened with the imminent danger of war and which wishes to defend itself, should bring in troops in the area to the terrain which is the forefront of its defence vis-a-vis the enemy, which is concentrating its forces and building up its forces on the other side of the border? Is that logical for you as an officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The build-up of forces began very early on. It began after Christmas. The deployment, of course, in Kosovo started before Christmas, and it continued throughout that period, well before we left. There was certainly a slight increase or an increase just prior to us leaving, but Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the -- your major forces were already in place long before the speculation began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday on several occasions that there had been an increase in our forces in March, and several times you mentioned the month in March, in actual fact, and as you know, March is quite a long way after Christmas. Do you remember what you were saying yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly remember what I was saying, and I was saying that we saw the T72s arrive in March. And as I just said a few seconds ago, there was an acceleration in March, but your forces were arriving from -- from January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So in March, the build-up of forces increased, and as you know, in March the NATO pact aggression took place on Yugoslavia. Is that something that is known to you or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me whether I knew that the bombing started in March?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I said the NATO pact aggression began in March against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the bombing did start in March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, our forces came in in March. And that was quite obviously the 11th hour for preparing our defence forces for the defence, because the war against Yugoslavia started in March. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were already preparing your defences at the end of February and the beginning of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's up to us. It's our affair to prepare for defence. I assume that a country that is faced with an aggression has the legitimate right to prepare for its defence. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I hope we've cleared up the question that at the time when the discussions were held, the talks were held that you indicated and which you claim had to do with the preparation of the mission's withdrawal from Kosovo and Metohija, that it was quite certain that an aggression, a NATO pact aggression against Yugoslavia was imminent. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've been over this as far as we can, and this witness really can't add anything more to what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, if that is so and as it is obvious, I should hope, is it then clear that an officer giving out information, alleged information, about a possible operation on the part of its own forces and gives it to the enemy's side in that way jeopardises the lives of tens of thousands of his colleagues and friends? Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, this is all comment by you. What you can ask the colonel is this: Did it occur to you that this official was jeopardising lives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The action to which this official was referring was an action against the KLA. He wasn't divulging any plans, preparation plans, at all of what might be coming after our departure. Had I passed this information to the KLA, and yes, it would have jeopardised the term. By this time I had a very good working relationship with the Commission for Cooperation and confidentiality was important. I had a respect for the commission and a respect for this person. And therefore, my respect grew from the fact that, as a liaison officer to this commission, I did not divulge anything from this commission back to the KLA. If I saw something on the Serbian side, I did not report this to the opposition as I did not report anything ever that I saw of KLA preparations to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it's clear to you, and we can see from what took place, and we also see this from the statements of the so-called commanders of these terrorist KLA groups, that NATO Air Force were the air forces of the KLA because they actually worked in cahoots together. Is that something you're aware of or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is getting well away from the witness's evidence, and it's a matter of comment by you. And if you have evidence of it, you can call it in due course. Colonel, can you assist as to this: It's alleged that the KLA and NATO were working together. As far as you were concerned, was there any evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, are you bringing into question the claim that NATO was the enemy's side vis-a-vis Yugoslavia and the KLA was likewise the enemy's side? Are you challenging those assertions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for me to challenge assertions. Now, you are here to question this witness. You can do so. But if you simply continue to make assertions, you'll be stopped. Now, the witness has dealt, as far as he can, with various assertions and questions you've made. Now, have you got anything else you want to ask him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I want to ask him some more things because I consider the facts to be indisputable, that NATO and the KLA together were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. You can make speeches in due course. Now, confine yourself to questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked my question on the basis of the fact that -- that is to say, I'm asking that this official who allegedly showed him the map must have realised that by doing so, he would have threatened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been over this. It is an abuse of the process for you to make speeches, Mr. Milosevic, at this stage. It's also an abuse to go over the same ground. Now, can we go over something else?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very important topic, because it is quite obvious that there's another manipulation of this false indictment to compensate and to soften --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are not -- these are not questions. Now, if you want to go on asking -- cross-examining this witness, you must do so properly, Mr. Milosevic. Now, move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. May I then just ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in all 78 days of the NATO aggression, NATO succeeded in destroying only eight tanks belonging to the Yugoslav army in the 70 days of its bombing? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm aware of is what I was told by your officers when I arrived in June, was that you had destroyed -- you claim to have destroyed 13. How many wrecks and damaged tanks you drew, we didn't see, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now I'm asking you as a military man, as an expert. If you, your side, had had information from this alleged map that you got concerning the operations of the Yugoslav forces, would those losses have been necessarily much bigger? Because you claim that you got this map which had the deployment of the Yugoslav forces and the places where they would operate, and I believe that this is sufficient information. So had you really had this, wouldn't these losses have had to be bigger or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an impossible question to answer for many reasons. In the first place, the activity was throughout Kosovo, even though it might have been concentrated in certain areas. We did not have any time lines, any time scales that we knew where you would be. We had no details, exact details of the operations. We had no people actually in Kosovo who were being able to sort of spot targets or look at targets; therefore, reconnaissance was extremely difficult. And I'm not denying that you have very well-trained and very professional forces who make -- who are probably one of the best armies, best trained armies in Europe, and therefore, they are very skilful at camouflage, at diversion, and giving any enemy, as you would call them, a hard time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, isn't it clear that had you had this information that you claim you had had, the losses of the Yugoslav forces would have had to be bigger? Because you claim that you had information about the actual places of attack, about the dynamics of the attack involved, and that you had received this kind of map. And we all know what these maps look like. And wouldn't the losses have had to be bigger than eight tanks in 78 days of bombings, bombings day in, day out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That seems to be the same question as you asked before. The map, as I understand it, Colonel, was related to how the KLA were to be dealt with. It had nothing to do with NATO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was NATO mentioned in your conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only in the last part, where the reference was made to the expulsion of the civilians, that it would save NATO a job later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't it seem illogical to you that a Yugoslav officer would claim that NATO would have work to do because of civilian expulsions, and NATO was finding a pretext in this way to attack Yugoslavia? Is this officer a moron? I mean, why would he say this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That sounds like a comment. Yes, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that your superior, also a British general, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Drewienkiewicz, the day before yesterday, in response to two of my direct questions, also under oath, stated that there was no plan against the Albanian population and that there were no indications of the existence of any kind of plan to expel the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have no idea what General Drewienkiewicz said yesterday during his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask this witness if he knew of such a plan or if there were any indications.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he claims that the answer is yes, and I am claiming that he is not telling the truth, because I'm saying that had he known this, Drewienkiewicz, who was his superior, would have had to know this, which doesn't work the other way around, that is, that he had to know everything that Drewienkiewicz knew. So therefore, there is no doubt that his superior had to know what he knew, because it was the witness's job to inform his superior about every important piece of information, and this information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. One question you can ask out of all of that, which is mainly a comment: Did you tell the general about this conversation? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did relate the conversation to General DZ, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is clear that Drewienkiewicz would have had to say that there was at least some indication that what this witness is claiming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This witness can't answer for the other witness. It's a pure comment. You can make it in due course. Meanwhile, you must ask questions which he can deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the witness confirmed that he did inform Drewienkiewicz about this, and Drewienkiewicz claimed that there were no indications of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that this person you mentioned - don't worry, I'm not going to utter the name itself - the person that you mentioned could not have had any kind of combat-related information, even that concerning a plan of attack against the KLA? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I gave -- said in my evidence, this man was on the commission. He was very aware of what went on throughout Kosovo. He knew of all operations that were taking place. He had a huge amount of experience. And I can't believe for one second that he wouldn't actually know what was -- what was going on from that part of the operation. It's not credible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know -- now, why am I asking you this? Do you know that the Commission for Cooperation with the KVM, that is to say with you, its members and the mission itself, including the head of the mission and the members of the mission were not in the chain of command at all, either in terms of the army or the -- the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always took the members of the commission to be representatives of the government, the army, and the police, because if we ever wanted access or information from the police, we would speak to the members of the commission. If we wanted to know anything at all about the military dispositions, about future intentions, activities which had taken place, we also spoke to the military on this commission. And therefore, we -- what else could we assume is that -- but that these people were actually spokesmen for their services and spokesmen for the government? What was the purpose of the mission otherwise?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people are precisely what you said now. Their purpose was to cooperate with your mission, that is to say, they conveyed your requests, and they asked on your behalf the appropriate commands or authorities for certain things that you had asked for. Do you remember that yesterday you explained that when you came to the mission you no longer commanded your unit or you were not held responsible by any superior command in the British army? Didn't you explain that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the same goes -- can't you assume that the same thing goes for the members of the Commission for Cooperation, whose job is to cooperate with you, not to command units? For example, do you know that General Loncar, who was the head of the mission, did not even participate in meetings of military or police commanders? Or any members of the mission, for that matter. They were members of this commission. They were not persons in the chain of command. Are you aware of that or are you not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the members of the commission were very aware what was happening militarily. They knew what was happening in terms of police operations and military operations because they had an effect upon them. I don't see what commanding military units has got to do with this. All I'm saying is that they knew what was going on in Kosovo and what was planned for Kosovo. They don't have to command anything to have that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you yourself explained, and I hope that that was obvious from your practice as well, that every day you had meetings with them and that within 24 hours, they received from the appropriate authorities information as to what had happened so that you could exchange this, use it, verify it, et cetera. They were your partner in verification, and they had to obtain this information from some authorities. They didn't gather the information themselves. Doesn't this seem logical to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's logical. It means that they had to speak to the military and to the commanders -- and to the police commanders to know what was going on. So they had contacts and knowledge about what was happening, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel, if you make your answer more simple, we can get on more easily. The question put to you was not whether they were -- Mr. Loncar and some other officials were aware of the fact which was happening at the time, rather the question was this: Whether they were in chain of command or not. You can make the answer simpler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were obviously not in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware that in our army, and I hope in other armies, too, that there is the principle of single seniority, and whoever is not in the chain of command cannot have available any kind of information that has to do with the future activity of any particular unit.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about this principle in your army, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that there cannot be lateral commanding? There can only be a single chain of command. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of it, of the existence of a chain of command, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that our Commission for Cooperation with you, although it consisted of some officers as well, it was, nevertheless, a civilian commission too?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware that it was purely a civilian commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that General Loncar was a retired general, therefore a civilian?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that General Loncar was a retired general and a civilian and he was replaced by General Brankovic who was a serving general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that later. And do you know how come General Loncar, who was a retiree, came to that position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that he came to this position at the request of William Walker, head of the mission, that he addressed to me personally, and that is because he had very good experience from his cooperation with General Loncar in Eastern Slavonia, and he wanted someone whom he knew well, whom he trusted, and whom he appreciated as an honest man and a good person to work with. He wanted to cooperate with him again. So this was an expression of our goodwill that we asked General Loncar to head this commission. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Otherwise, I see that you do not know about this. However, I have to put this as a question to you because I have been asked to act that way. Do you know that General Brankovic did not replace General Loncar actually?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You surprise me, Mr. Milosevic, because General Brankovic introduced himself, and I was introduced to the new commission with General Brankovic as the head of this new commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You probably understood each other that way, just like when you were saying that you were replacing Donna Phelan; it was somebody else. However, General Loncar did not leave the commission. Until the 23rd of May, he was the vice-chairman of this federal commission of ours and he was that all the time and head of the mission in Kosovo. And General Brankovic was not General Loncar's superior. On the contrary, it was General Loncar who was the superior of General Brankovic. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I was concerned, General Brankovic announced himself as the boss of the commission and he was the person we spoke to. And he was present at all the meetings, not General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Brankovic replaced Colonel Kotur, not General Loncar. And you were in charge of cooperation on military matters but also within the function of this civilian mission, not within any kind of military function. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's no good arguing with the witness. You can call your evidence if it's different, but you've heard his evidence. He's said that Brankovic was in charge. That's his evidence. Now, in due course, if you want to rebut it, you can, but there's no point going on arguing. That is the way that time is wasted in cross-examination, why we have to impose these time limits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The matter is that I want to ascertain here how much this witness actually knows from all the things that he has been claiming to know, and obviously, he doesn't know that much. What I am presenting here are undeniable facts with regard to these appointments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not presenting anything. You're asking questions. Now, if you want to test his knowledge of the commission in some other way, do so, but there's no point going on about Brankovic because he's given his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, this is just an example, it's of no major significance. The matter is that he is ill-informed, and he drew the wrong conclusions. Do you know that this commission had a coordinating role only within the framework of cooperation with the OSCE, to coordinate this cooperation between the OSCE and the Yugoslav authorities in charge? This was a Commission for Cooperation. That was its name. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a mission for cooperation, not a mission for coordination, as you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cooperation. In order to cooperate, you have to have coordination between the organs that are cooperating. Isn't that logical? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who the chairman of the commission of the federal government for cooperation with the mission was and how many members this commission had?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the commission chaired by General Loncar?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a commission of the federal government. Loncar was its vice-chairman, and the seat of this commission was in Pristina. However, on the whole, the commission that was appointed by the federal government - and this was no secret because decisions of the federal government are published in the Official Gazette and are therefore public - do you know who the president of the commission was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only commission that I knew about was the commission headed by General Loncar in Pristina. That was the level that I worked at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General Pellnas in Belgrade, who also communicated on behalf of your mission with headquarters in Belgrade, who did he liaise with if there was only what was in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea who General Pellnas is, and this is the first time I've heard his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Swedish general who was also your representative in Belgrade, and he communicated with the government in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bo Pellnas.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. I misunderstand the pronunciation. I did see him. He was working in Belgrade, yes. He was our representative to your government in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he communicated with the commission headquarters in Belgrade, that is to say, this commission that was set up by the federal government.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. And he found his work, I believe, so difficult that he eventually resigned and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know, since I hope that we have explained the civilian nature of this commission that worked with you, and we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You put points when you should be asking questions, which are tendentious, argumentative. Do you agree that it was a civilian commission or not, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a joint civilian-military-police commission, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that this alleged map that you have been referring to, which obviously did not exist after all, or any map, according to the rules of service, could not have been carried out of the operations department of the unit that it belonged to, even if it were a map of a pure exercise only?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the map that he pointed out, the outline of manoeuvre?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh. So you are speaking about a map that is actually an outline of manoeuvre?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map that I was shown was a blank map, and he pointed out on this map how the operation and the manoeuvre would take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh. Now we've come to a new fact. On a plain map, he showed you with his hand how activities would be carried out against the KLA. So that is what we have asserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was his evidence, as I recollect it, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you say yesterday, because obviously my understanding was different because you kept talking about this map and this plan, and now it turns out that there was no plan, that he was showing you on a geography map how the attack against the KLA would take place. Do you still claim that this officer told you that there was a plan to expel the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He showed me on the military map the plan how to -- how they would deal with the KLA, and then said they would also expel the civilian population, yes. Not part -- not as part of this military operation. That was to come later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say this to you in connection with a plan? Did he say that there was a plan or was this his personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, the -- the plan of operation, plan of the manoeuvre against the KLA, were not -- could not have been just his personal opinion, and he did not give me that impression. He said, "This is how we would do it; this is how we will do it. And this is -- when this is completed we will expel the Albanians." I have no idea. I cannot tell you what he was thinking, exactly whether -- I can't be inside his head. I just do not know whether it was his personal plan, but I doubt it, because the plan was so detailed and it then took place in that -- the general manoeuvre actually happened that way, well, he must either have been clairvoyant or he knew about it. And why then should he make another comment which is untrue or just his wishes or his hopes? When he's just given me one factual bit of information, I presumed the second piece of information was also factual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, when he said that, did you follow it up with a request for further information or elaboration or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The impression I had, Your Honour, was that he had already told me far too much. What he told me was virtually in hushed tones over the map, and I knew it wasn't the time or the place to actually try and elaborate on that, and I could tell from his manner that he wasn't prepared to elaborate on that. That was all he was prepared to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The elimination of KLA units, at all events, would, regardless of this statement of yours about the talk, be a legitimate task of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the elimination of the KLA be a legitimate task of the Yugoslav forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose if you were at war with the KLA, then yes. I don't know -- I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's probably a matter for us. It's a matter of law if it's legitimate or not. Mr. Milosevic, you've been now two hours with this witness, so if there are other topics you want to cover with him, you should do so now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are very many topics, and I hope that you're not going to interrupt my cross-examination this time too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll interrupt it if it's not proper. If you ask proper questions, it won't be interrupted. And one thing you should remember is that the questions should be short, and that way we'll get through more topics.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me follow on from my previous question. In the KLA, did the KLA play the role of NATO infantry in the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see the statements made by their commanders such as Thaci, Haradinaj, and the others, who precisely bear out what I said a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer. He said no. If you've got some evidence to the contrary, you can call it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to prolong my questions about this quite obviously rigged Prosecution issue with respect to the map, I demand of you that the witness who was mentioned by -- the person that this witness, this lieutenant colonel mentioned, the witness who allegedly talked to him and gave him this information should be heard here and that you will issue all guarantees to him that he will not be detained and so on and so forth. And I am asking for this, for him to be protected, because there is a lot of dirt thrown at an officer of the Yugoslav army that he supplied the enemy, prior to the aggression, with this information. He was smeared. And as you know, what we're talking about here will not be a secret for all times. And the man has children and grandchildren, and his name should not be smeared by a rigged-up thing of this kind. So I am asking that this witness be heard here in the courtroom along with all the protective measures for secrecy that can be accorded him, because all this is a fabrication, a pure fabrication, and that is quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with this witness at all. If you have an application, you can make it. Now, meanwhile, let us conclude this cross-examination. In my own view, you should have no more than a further hour, which will give you the same as the Prosecution. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it would be fair for me to be accorded more time than the Prosecution, because the Prosecution is able to prepare with countless associates and helpers, but I have to go through all this on my own, and this is all new ground for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That -- that -- that, Mr. Milosevic, we have in mind, that you are on your own and they are many more. We do consider that. But we also consider the time that's wasted in your making speeches and going over the same ground again and again. We balance the two in coming to a decision on how much time you should have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I hope that we will be able to devote a little more than an hour to this witness. I now have to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. see where I left off yesterday in his statement and testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your statement that it was not envisaged that the KLA should have its representative, but their positions put before the commission were put forward by others. Actually, I'm looking at page 3 of your statement, paragraph 2 from the bottom in the Serbian text, that this was put forward by Major David Wilson or another British officer. That sentence. "The KLA was never meant to have a representative present," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have his statement. Thank you. Yes, have you found the passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I wasn't aware there was a question. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What's the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was the following: What was the task of these people that had contacts with the KLA? As I can see from Drewienkiewicz's statement, he says that somebody else except for David Wilson worked in that area. Who were those other people?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: David Wilson and then later David Meyer, who was also British, worked directly with the KLA, liaised with the KLA and behalf of General DZ. I believe that other nations might have also had representatives with the KLA who would also try and talk to them and reason with them to prevent any confrontations, which is one of our acquired tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Drewienkiewicz says that there were two David Wilsons, both from Britain, and quite by chance, as he says, both were liaison officers with the KLA. One David Wilson worked as a liaison officer with the KLA from Pristina and the other as a liaison officer for the KLA from Prizren. This other one, as representative of KVM, was a representative in Rambouillet. Now, that's what Drewienkiewicz says. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly am. David Wilson, as you say, the taller one who worked at Prizren, was the KLA liaison officer in the Prizren area only, and he was the one we sent to Rambouillet. And David Wilson, the smaller one, was based on DZ's staff and worked directly to General DZ as the -- within the headquarters of the OSCE. So he was responsible for liaising with all the OSCE KLA liaison staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he convey information to the KLA and back from the KLA? Was that a two-way feedback, two-way information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would negotiate on behalf of DZ with the KLA and pass information, which was important to prevent any activities, any actions, or any misunderstandings, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He did not give out information to the KLA in connection with -- that is to say, with respect to the terrorist activities that they were carrying out, he didn't use that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would not pass any information that was sensitive. So, for example, if he heard during a meeting with the Commission for Cooperation at the headquarters that there was a Serbian convoy coming down, that's the sort of information he would not pass. If there was information being sought by the Serbian side, then this information would be passed back and any information that the KLA could give back would be passed back to the Serbian commission, the Commission for Cooperation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was his role -- give us a yes or no answer to save time, please. Was his role to insist that the KLA adhere to the cease-fire, that is to say, not to launch attacks? Was that his function or was his only purpose to inform?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We also had the function of telling them not to participate in any of these actions. We tried to prevent both sides from any action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say on that same page, in the following paragraph: "It is my upon that Loncar and his subordinates really saw the OSCE/FRY Commission for Cooperation and the KVM as a means of proving to the world that they were the innocent party, but they were very specific as to what they wanted us to verify." Is it not logical that under a conflict, when you had conflicts with terrorist units and groups, that the government was acting legitimately and is the innocent party when it is exposed to terrorism, terrorism towards the police, the organs of power and authority, and the citizens themselves? Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Will you answer that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just wondering how many questions were in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, pick one and answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, in a conflict, for example, the -- if you are being attacked by terrorist groups, of course a government does have the power and the right to defend itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what else did the government do but protect civilians and representatives of the government from terrorists?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the things it did, it used disproportionate force on many occasions. And these were the sort of events that they would not wish us to verify, but they were very happy for us to verify if they had been attacked by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they helped you to verify all the other cases that took place in the field. That was not brought into question, and we saw that from the reports. But answer me this, please: What does it mean what you say at the end of that paragraph, where you say that they really did consider the cooperation to be beneficial because they were the innocent party? And at the end of that paragraph, you state the following: You're talking about Loncar, and you say that it would appear that he never understood the OSCE/KVM, and that quite obviously he found -- he was irritated by the fact that he could not force -- he was irritated by the fact that he could not force the OSCE and the KVM -- he couldn't get them to say bad things about the KLA. He was obviously annoyed that he couldn't get the OSCE and the KVM to say bad things about the KLA. That's what you say. Now, does that -- is that clearly -- does it clearly show your biasness with respect to the KLA, that is to say, to the advantage and on the KLA's side? Yes or no; were you biased or not? So he couldn't get you to say anything bad, any bad things about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think again, Mr. Milosevic, you've asked me several questions here. When I say that he never seemed to come to grips with the OSCE and he was obviously annoyed he couldn't get us to say bad things about the KLA, you have to expand that to say, that we wrote daily reports, and if there was a KLA terrorist attack which killed innocent people, innocent policemen, soldiers, we made these press releases. We don't have any control over the press. If the press refuse to publish these, for some unknown reason, that was not within our gift. But every action, every activity was passed to the press office, who then passed it to the press authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you well known of the Glodjani KLA torture sites where tens of people were thrown into Radonjic Lake, and did you know about the mass sites of Serb -- Serb suffering? Are all these crimes things that quite simply have to make oneself ask what it means when you state that he was annoyed that he couldn't get the OSCE and KVM to say bad things about the KLA? Don't you know about all the crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a speech. You're asked, Colonel, about Glodjani, the site there. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were asked about Radonjic Lake. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered these questions as best he can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's a very good thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the following page, you talk about the 27th of December and the tension. I don't want to mention for what reasons. You spoke about that yesterday. The KLA took a farmer prisoner, a Serb farmer, and opened fire on the police, seriously wounding several policemen. You state that yourself here: "They were holding a Serb farmer, Dragoslav Zdravkovic. A MUP patrol had gone in to rescue the farmer but had come under fire and sustained heavy injuries." Those are your words, I am reading from your statement. Loncar informed you that the army had ordered tanks to enter and that the MUP would lead the attack and so on and so forth, because he was annoyed -- he was irritated and very angry and keen for the VJ and MUP to carry out the attack, as you state. So he informed you what they were supposed to do. And then you go on to say, "And challenged us to go in ourselves." What does that mean that "he challenged us to go in ourselves"? Wasn't it your business to verify it? So he called upon you and he challenged you. That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he said was that we should go in there, sort it out, and bring him out. Therefore, he challenged us. It certainly was not our -- part of our agreement, according to the agreement, to actually carry out operations and negotiate hostage releases. We were the Kosovo Verification Mission. However, our mission began to change direction like this, and if we could help and if we were prepared to stick our necks out, but as an unarmed force, we were prepared to do it in order to prevent any conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is the following: Yesterday in your oral testimony, you spoke about this incident on the 27th of December, and you said precisely that it was an incident carried out by the army and police. That's what you said. And then we saw what the incident was about, in actual fact, that it was of a Serb farmer that had been held and that the police had been wounded, and you yourself mentioned yesterday that there were one to two thousand members of the KLA with a whole truckload of ammunition. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it possible to say, given this situation, that the KLA, with ammunition and thousands, that a Serb farmer was held and wounded? Is it possible to say that the Serb forces caused that particular incident as you said so yesterday? Is it possible for you to say that? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Of course they didn't cause it. The Serb forces did not cause the incident, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that is precisely what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't remember him saying that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, take a look at the transcript and you'll find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And everything ended in a normal fashion, with the understanding of whatever, but we're not going to waste time on that now. Then you go on to talk about the meeting that was held afterwards, and you say that Sainovic hurled a whole load of insults at you and said Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the Serbs had the right to use the force they did. I assume that he could not have said it that way, but he might have said that he had -- they had the right to act against terrorists and that he said -- and you said, "We were not doing the verification honourably and accused us of smuggling weapons and include the Americans and Germans, et cetera." Now, was that not correct? Was it not so? Was it not true that certain members of the Verification Mission undertook spying tasks, including helping the KLA to smuggle weapons? Is that true or is it not? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this smuggling of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were an expert in weapons. Do you know where the weapons came from, where the KLA got their weapons from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the weapons came across the mountains from Albania, by mule trains and by humans, humans carrying them across the mountains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you go on to explain, as an example of Sainovic's capacity to get things done was when, during that meeting, we asked to be permitted to visit about 11 KLA prisoners. Now, can you even assume that Sainovic as president of the Commission for Cooperation would be able to do this? That is to say, in order for him to be able to accomplish this, he would have to ask the Minister of Justice for permission to do that. He wouldn't be able to do it on us own back without permission.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that he would have to refer it but he gave us every indication that this would be done and, later that evening, we were given permission to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. The commission decided to do what you had asked because it was logical and that's what you did. Then you go on to explain, towards the end of that paragraph, the following: That Sainovic could speak on behalf of Belgrade and Loncar could only affect local matters. What is illogical there? Why should not political issues go via politicians and what is illogical in the fact that the Vice-Premier should see to political issues? Is there any mystery there in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what does this whole description mean about Colonel Kotur having a camouflage uniform, that he was from an elite special unit? He was sent to the commission by the General Staff of the army, who was the sole competent authority to give representatives for civilian matters just as it puts forward people for being military attaches in an embassy, for example. Do you know that they could have taken any uniform? They could have worn a marine uniform, a naval uniform, had you been by the sea, on the sea, and that his uniform did not note any affiliation to any special unit of any kind.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was trying to get at here was actually he was actually wearing a uniform, as was Colonel Mijatovic at meetings and therefore this indicated that this was not a purely civilian mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he wore what he found comfortable, and he might have worn a civilian -- civilian clothing too, just like Colonel Mijatovic could have worn anything, a police uniform, whereas he was in civilian clothing. For his function and post in the mission, it had no bearing, it was of no importance. And none of them, as a member of the commission, could have commanded anything. We've cleared up this point about your mistaken conclusions as to the structure of the mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's just a comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All right. I'm just looking at something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what is the point of your assertion here that at the football stadium there was a piste for helicopters, helicopter takeoffs and landings. Are you aware of the fact that this stadium in Pristina for helicopters was the only spot near the centre where helicopters were able to land and that helicopters had landed there for decades, 20 years ago, 30 years ago? I myself landed there 25 years ago on that runway in that same spot. Where else can you land in Pristina unless you want to land in the middle of the city square with the kiosks selling frankfurters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't want to know about the kiosks selling frankfurters. Now, is the point of this that it is the only helicopter landing place in Pristina? Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Why then all this mystification and linking it up to the proximity of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's put it to the witness. It's what's said is that this was the only helicopter landing place and there was nothing sinister or anything of that sort in it being close to the MUP headquarters. Can you assist us as to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an airport not far way where helicopters also landed but this was a convenient place in the middle of town, the only place, adjacent to the MUP headquarters and the VJ headquarters and most of the flights were either government flights or MUP or VJ. It's as straightforward as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's quite clear. The airport is quite a distance from town. Now, on page 7 of your statement, some observations are made which bring into question your assertion about the impossibility of you going about your business, and I'm going to quote both these points. You say: "Whenever I encountered a problem of going to a certain area, I would call up Mijatovic --" and you're referring to Colonel Mijatovic, member of the commission, Loncar's. "... I would call Mijatovic on the phone and he would then contact the local MUP commander who would then give us permission to pass. Mijatovic also helped us to access certain police stations. On the 17th of March, 1999, at a meeting with Mijatovic, he informed me that he had come into contact with all the command points of MUP and introduced procedure which would ensure us to have access," et cetera. And then several paragraphs after that, you say the following: "Kotur showed me a letter from Major General Lazarevic, that is the commander of the Pristina Corps at that time, which ordered all VJ units to give access to KVM patrols." So even when we're talking about the police force and the army, you had orders enabling you to move around without any impediment. Can you then speak of a refusal to cooperate or efforts to thwart successful cooperation and to make it impossible for you to perform your tasks? From what yourself have written, is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents that you refer to and the access was done at that level. However, it was never -- it was never passed down to the units on the ground, and therefore we could stand for as long as we wanted to try to get into certain areas, open areas of ground which the VJ or the MUP were holding, and we could not get in. I was one of the few people with a satellite telephone who could ring Colonel Mijatovic and say, "I am at this location. I have a commander with me, can you please remind him of the agreement that we have, the letter that you -- that General Lazarevic had produced to give us access. And then grudgingly, after a long time, we'd be allowed through. But this access was not general -- the letters were not disseminated, and the access was very, very -- extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're going to -- the time's come for the adjournment, but if you want to make one more point, you can. Ask one more question, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was just following on from what the witness said. You said that you had this surprise factor with your patrols in touring and inspecting certain points. How can you surprise somebody if you can move around without anybody's -- if you don't have the permission to move around? You said that you surprised them. You took them by surprise when you conducted your inspections. Now, if you were able to surprise someone, that implies that you have freedom of movement. Now, is that in contradiction to what you said that you were unable to move around and that you didn't have permission and access?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no contradiction whatsoever. The surprise inspection was carried out along the main roads, whereas your units were not positioned, your major units were not positioned on the main roads. They were positioned around villages, in the countryside, and therefore there can be no contradiction. There are two -- they're two separate events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before you rise, in relation to the next witnesses, the Chamber will recall I said a couple of days ago it was possible that we might seek to call not K22 first but the first 92 bis witnesses. All the witness are here, but because K22, who originally made arrangements to come before the Easter break before the timetable changed only arrived last evening, it will not be possible to have helpful and complete summary of his evidence, I think, until tomorrow. He's here, and the summary is in the process of final preparation, but I don't think it will be ready until tomorrow. So if this witness fishes, I would ask that we take one, at least, of the 92 bis witnesses first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, 1999, you were in the area of Decani Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with the representatives of the MUP when it was agreed that the KVM should escort the MUP to that area when there would be a change of shifts at their forward posts. This was done because you wanted to check lest there be any reinforcements at the forward posts. Then the KVM were shot at for a while. The way you had put it then, it was unclear as to who had done the shooting. That was your position, that it was unclear. Wasn't it obvious that it only could have been the KLA, because you were accompanied by the police and it was quite obvious that the police would not shoot at a convoy that they were escorting themselves? Why was it your assessment that it was unclear as to who had done the shooting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall saying that I was unclear. I was very clear that the shooting had taken place by the -- by the KLA, and the -- I believe Ramush admitted later that this was the case. He apologised for wounding two of my people, and put it down to the fact that they thought we were Serb secret police driving around in what appeared to be OSCE vehicles leading the convoy into this forward position, and that's why they had done it. So it was the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That is only a direct statement of the KLA, something that could have made you give up on your original thought that you did not know who had done the shooting and that suspicion could be cast on both sides.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the initial stages for the first 24, 36 hours, we had no idea who'd done the shooting, and we couldn't imagine any reason at the time why the KLA should wish to shoot at orange vehicles. Therefore, it was unclear. We just couldn't work out why the Serb, the MUP, or the VJ would want to shoot at us, and we couldn't figure out why the KLA would to want to shoot at us. It wasn't normal for us to be shot at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was less clear to you why the KLA would be shooting at you than why the army would be shooting at you. What you are saying now, isn't that the most specific kind of evidence of your partiality as far as the KLA is concerned? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not partiality because we were shot at. Even I was shot at, or shots were fired in my direction, to keep me out of certain areas by your forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were our forces doing, shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Even the Podujevo on -- east of Gornja Lapastica, there was an occasion where we were told not to go somewhere because we would be shot at by the KLA and the area was unsafe. We then saw one of your vehicles deliberately move around, and we saw the shots being fired from that vehicle in our general direction to frighten us, to prove to us that it was dangerous and we shouldn't be there. This was one of your control methods to make sure that we did not venture where you didn't want us to go, because most verifiers were civilians and they were afraid of being shot at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But now you're saying that shooting could have taken place but it didn't. So did this vehicle shoot at you or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This MUP vehicle that you mentioned just now, did it shoot at you or did it not shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did shoot at us, yes. On a previous occasion. Not the 15th of January occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it hit someone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The intention was to frighten us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were shooting into the air to frighten you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is this not mentioned in any one of the Verification Mission reports, this kind of incident, that somebody was shooting in your direction? I mean, from the security forces of Yugoslavia and the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you will find that it was reported on numerous occasions in the OSCE reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you going to assert now that there were occasions when the army and the police shot at the verifiers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's what he's been saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. These are new facts indeed, and I bring them into question, absolutely. There is an assertion among your sources that all evidence was presented to the chief of mission so that he could establish whether some act would be a violation of the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement. The Head of Mission had the exclusive right to ascertain whether a particular act was a violation of this agreement. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what purpose did you serve, all of you, all the verifiers, if it was only your chief, William Walker, who could decide whether a particular act was a violation or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could all easily see whether something was a violation. Therefore, we could report this violation to William Walker, who would then pass it through official channels, through Bo Pellnas or directly to General Loncar or via Keller to Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was only Walker who could assess what a violation was and what was not a violation. Nobody else from the mission could do that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, he was the chief, and therefore any sort of reporting upwards went under his signature, I mean went under his authority. He was our chief. However, if I went to a meeting and I was authorised to say something was a violation, I would say it at the meeting with General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Walker the only person who was authorised to accept or not accept a particular member of the mission to carry out his duties or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose he was ultimately responsible, as the boss, but I shouldn't think for one second that Walker was involved in selecting every member of the mission of 1.400-odd people, plus another 1.500 civilians. He wouldn't be doing anything but vetting people's applications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of a particular case when the Deputy Head of Mission was appointed, the one who was in charge of police and judiciary, Giovani Kesler [phoen], an Italian judge, he was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that he was appointed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But there is an explanation here, that he said that when verifying police standards, the international community should not do anything that should upset the Serb authorities. And Walker refused to accept his appointment so the post remained vacant for a longer amount of time. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were supposed to get 40 verifiers for the police, but then only ten arrived subsequently. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had difficulties in recruiting policemen who could be released from their duties in their countries and come to Kosovo. These weren't the only verifiers we had difficulty in recruiting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fact that he refused an Italian because he said that the Serbian police should be treated properly, that is what is contained in the statement of your boss Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness does not know anything about this.
