utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am making him aware of it because he's not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're not going to get anywhere with this sort of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at one place in your statement that you found out later that NATO had intercepted radio communications showing that Serbs were more deeply involved in the alleged slaughter - you're talking about Racak - than they had admitted, and that they had actually issued orders for these people to be killed. You -- what kind of interception is this? Because you say you found out, that you learned about this. What is this that you learned about this interception of some conversation that indicates that somebody had given orders to have these people killed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from several sources who commented to me that. Because I myself was interested as to the truthfulness of this whole event, and I was sort of playing devil's advocate at one point, and I was told, you know, "We can assure you that there has been information provided from signals, radio intercepts." I presume these must have been intercepts in Macedonia or somewhere nearby where these conversations had been overheard. This is something I was told. This is something that -- these are not documents that I have actually read or held in my hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the only thing I wish to clarify. In your statement, you also said the MUP and the army of Yugoslavia always called the members of the KLA terrorists. Do you think that they were terrorists or do you think that they were not terrorists?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were some terrorists, and there were also a great number of people who were village militia, people who were sort of guarding their properties and their families. So, yes, some of the people you referred to as the KLA, I have no doubt that they carry out terrorists activities and behave as terrorists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were you bothered then by the fact that the military and the police were calling them terrorists? Because you knew yourself that they were terrorists.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this tag was being applied to virtually all Albanians. It wasn't specific, the number of small terrorist cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, these people who were shooting at the military and at the police, were they terrorists or were they not terrorists? Those who planted bombs underneath buses and marketplaces and shops, were they terrorists or were they not terrorists?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were terrorists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are saying that there was coordination between the army and the police, and you also say that this was organised. And if it were to be organised, the lowest level would have to be the level of major, the rank of major. This is your expert opinion. I'm not challenging it. But my question is: Is it logical if there is both army and police in a certain area, that they should know where they all are and that it's normal for the army to know where the police is and for the police to know where the army is? Isn't this logical for you because they belong to one and the same state?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said major because major is usually a battalion commander in your forces, and yes, it's logical that they should know what each are doing and therefore there is general knowledge of what is happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is something that is quite logical in terms of the behaviour of any police or army. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described an event after the incident on the Podujevo-Pristina road when an army patrol was ambushed and when a colonel was killed. You say the army of Yugoslavia then brought the tanks in and closed in on the village and then threw up an outer cordon about one or two kilometres away and then an inner cordon with the tanks and then sent the infantry in to search the town for the sniper. There were no retributions, no destruction, and no killings. Do you consider this to be a logical and normal act on the part of the military? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason I put this statement in was to actually show that when the VJ had carried out an operation, they actually performed this within all the legal frameworks and acted humanely and decently, and also performed well as a military unit, in contrast to what the MUP did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are talking about the role of the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija, and you are talking about the kind of role it had, on the basis of which you've been saying, it is your assertion that it did not have a police role. You even say that they were not involved in regulating traffic, in combatting crime, et cetera. Did you see any traffic police during all that time, during your stay in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- during my time in Pristina, I did see a few ordinary policemen in the streets, carrying out their duties and occasionally controlling traffic as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it clear to you that these policemen who controlled traffic are also members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how can you say, then, that the MUP did not perform these functions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority -- I only saw a few policemen carrying out these functions. All other MUP, 99 per cent of the MUP I saw in Kosovo, were performing a military function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In searching for terrorists, murderers, those who plant bombs, is that a military or a police function?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a function in which the -- the police have primacy, and if they require, for example as in Northern Ireland where now we work against the terrorists, we use the army in support. But they carry out an investigative type of operation, the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in this case, the police is carrying out investigative operations and looking for the perpetrators of crimes. Is that clear or is that not clear?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the methodology is different, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to traffic, what do you think? Who else but the police could have been searching for perpetrators of crimes, arresting criminals, looking for perpetrators of murders, looting, all other criminal offences? Who else could have been doing that except for the police? Because it is your claim that the police was not carrying out those functions.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the police responsibility to carry out those functions, but all the activities that we observed that MUP carried out were typical military, infantry, armoured, dismounted, infantry type of procedures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wrote here in your statement that there were local policemen and members of the traffic police who did not belong to the MUP. They wore regular police uniforms with white belts -- that is what traffic policemen wear anyway so they would be more visible for all the participants in traffic -- and they just carried sidearms. The MUP wore combat outfits, et cetera, et cetera. It was your understanding that these were also members of the MUP. Isn't that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believe that the traffic police were a subdivision of -- a small subdivision of the MUP, but we referred to -- generally to the MUP as the people in combat kit with Kalashnikovs and webbing, helmets, et cetera, because they were -- 99 per cent of the MUP in Kosovo appeared to us to be these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of the MUP structure? MUP means Ministry of the Interior, Ministry of the Police. You're aware of that, aren't you? And do you know in that structure there is an administration for the traffic police, there is an administration for the combatting of crime, preventing crime, various other administrations, or departments, rather, for issuing passports, et cetera, et cetera. Are you aware of this entire structure, according to which the MUP caries out its regular duties just like any other police in the world?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were the people in the mission whose responsibility was understanding the structure. Mine was working, trying to sort of coordinate the activities, working on the ground and trying to sort of work the verification. Thank you for the explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me how you explain the fact that there were such great differences in the statement you give with respect to -- compared to the statement of your boss, Drewienkiewicz? For example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a matter for him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. These are vital differences, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in the monthly reports of the OSCE compiled on the basis of your daily and weekly reports about the situation in Kosovo from mid-January to mid-February 1999, that it states that in Kosovo, urban terrorism was on the rise?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly, but if that's what it says, then I accept it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is what you say in the statement also true, that the level of conflict was reduced but the KLA attacked the Serb police? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the KLA use to attack the army and MUP units with? Because your verification of weapons was -- also implied recording the types of weaponry, their deployment, and so on. So what did the KLA use to attack the army and MUP units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They obviously used Kalashnikov or -- a whole variety of assault rifles, ranging from Kalashnikovs to Armalites [phoen]. We even saw one person, who must have drawn the booby prize, with a British rifle. They obviously explosives, they used rocket-propelled grenades. They used mortars. These were the normal sniper rifles of large calibre, often American. This type of weapon or Russian Draganoff rifle. These were the type of weapons that the KLA would use as their weapon of choice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition to the mortars, did they also use hand-held launchers when attacking armoured vehicles, fortified positions and so on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What calibre of mortar did they use?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used -- at the beginning, they used a smaller calibre mortar, and towards the end, they had acquired a much larger calibre. So it ranged from 60 millimetres right up to 120.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they come by those mortars? How did they procure them? Because they're heavy ones, 120 millimetres. How were they able to get them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I know, sir, is that some of this equipment came over the border, over the mountains from the direction of Albania, but more than that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did they get American weapons that you mentioned a moment ago? How did they come by those?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in the course of 1998 and 1999, that is to say during the time your mission was there, the KLA effected a much larger number of terrorist attacks on the members of the army and the MUP and civilians, both Serbs and Albanians and Muslims as well, Romanies, Gorani, and all the others, than throughout the period of time that had gone before in the several years before that period? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that a great many attacks were carried out but I cannot give a qualitative assessment -- quantitative assessment. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now this fact, the precipitous increase in the number of attacks while your mission was there, was that the subject of your attention and your analysis at the meetings you had with Walker, Drewienkiewicz, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were topics that were discussed to see how we could persuade both sides to cease the hostilities and to reduce the number of deaths and attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you successful at all with the -- with the KLA in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe on occasion we were successful, and we managed to get the KLA to withdraw from certain forward positions after we had discussions with the Commission of Cooperation who asked us to remove, for example, near Podujevo, the whole line of hills. We did actually have the KLA agreement to pull away their snipers from the positions overlooking the road for quite a considerable time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As there was this drastic increase in terrorist attacks, how then were you able to report on the violation of agreement by the MUP when it was quite obvious that it was the KLA that did the violation in the first place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reported the violations as they came. So if -- if it was an attack launched by the KLA, we would clearly state this, that the KLA had shot, attacked, destroyed, and then we would also report the -- the subsequent Serbian action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the checkpoints, do you consider those to be a preventive or repressive operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason that Burns tried to keep the number of checkpoints down to a minimum was because a large number of checkpoints just prevented everyone from moving around Kosovo. And obviously I agree with you entirely that if the level of activity increases, then you can then be able to increase the number of control points and checkpoints. The number of checkpoints was always very large since our arrival. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself noted that you found and assessed as being a violation some 30-odd or 40 up to control points. Now, what does 40 control points mean on the whole territory of Kosovo and Metohija with 26 municipalities and several thousand settlements? Do you consider that to be an overly large number?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they control the movement of around -- the whole of Kosovo. Kosovo, as you know, Mr. Milosevic, has only a small number of main access roads that can be used throughout the year, and with 40 patrols, you can effectively close off and totally control and stop virtually the traffic moving in Kosovo. It's easily done with 40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was that not a necessity if it was -- if we had to uncover terrorists and their activities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is what you were doing and not just preventing movement, which it appeared you were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your mission endeavour to see that weapons are taken away from the terrorists in order to reduce the level of crime that was permanently high?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: (A) this was not a mandate, neither was it for us to take away your weapons as neither -- as it wasn't to take away their weapons. And we also weren't in any position, as an unarmed verification force, to carry this activity out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had an overview of all the positions of the army of Yugoslavia and the MUP of Yugoslavia and all the weaponry. You had a complete overall picture of the positions and weaponry of the army of Yugoslavia. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did have regular meetings with members of the Yugoslav commission, and you discussed these issues with them, did you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed this and the -- as I mentioned before several times, access to actually inspect or verify anything was rarely given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you told us all the types of weapons yesterday that the army disposed of, and identified them. So you had an insight into everything that you presented here.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was because we observed, very carefully, weapons coming in. For example, you did not declare that you had brought in new types of weapons, and when this was questioned, you said, "Well, they are much the same. A tank is a tank," I think the quotation was. "Like a woman is a woman," I believe the entire phrase went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you personally have meetings with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met them in the early stages. I -- because I was working near Podujevo and tried to negotiate with David Wilson, I met Remi, for example. And then later, the only meetings I had with the KLA would have been when I was given that authority by your government to visit the 11 prisoners in Nis. But my activity with the KLA virtually came to a standstill for the last couple of months. My main activity was cooperating and liaising with the VJ and the commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you visited those 11 that you just mentioned, did you -- were you able to see that conduct towards them was proper, that there were no problems with regard to their treatment in view of the fact that they were in prison?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw them, I had seen that they were now living in reasonable conditions and were well-dressed, but they recounted to me that they had all been given fairly unpleasant treatment in the period before my visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any traces on them of any kind of treatment of that kind, the treatment that you say they had experienced?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not ask them to undress and -- so I could inspect them. A lot of the ill-treatment was psychological, where, for example, prisoners were made to stand the entire day in their cells. They were not allowed to sit down or to lie down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what they told you, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the other hand, when they were set free, the soldiers, did they have any traces of beatings on them that were obvious? They didn't have to take their clothes off for it to become evident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the KLA or are you referring to the nine soldiers that were captured by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Serb soldiers, when they were set free. Did they have any traces of beatings on their person?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I saw the soldiers shortly after they'd been captured, one or two -- I videoed them and I passed the tapes to your commission, and yes, one or two of them did have marks about their faces where they had been beaten up, assaulted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the difference between what you saw when you saw the Albanians and what you saw with the Serb prisoners, there was a difference there. Now, have you ever been to Albania? Did you ever go to Albania during the duration of your mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the leaders of the KLA inform you of any of their intended activities? Did they make their plans known to you or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Haradinaj, in his interview, speaks about many meetings with English, American, German and other military representatives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This witness says he didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, all the reports that you sent out, did you send them out to the organs of Yugoslavia as well? To the Yugoslav authorities as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a system whereby our reports were passed to the Commission for Cooperation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the reports that you sent out were sent out to the Yugoslav authorities as well; is that right? That was your duty provided for by the agreement, because it says so, as you know.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we endeavoured to send as many reports as we could across to the commission. Certainly the reports were also sent to Bo Pellnas in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had the duty to send them on further to the Yugoslav authorities. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either he or the commission in Pristina, yes. Both. Either or.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that, to all practical intents and purposes, means that if somebody wasn't sent to the Yugoslav authorities, could not be treated as being an event, an incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can deal with that. Mr. Milosevic, you've now had over three hours, well over three hours with this witness. Another 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's difficult for me to find my way in all these questions in only 20 minutes, but I'll do my best and skip over some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the detained members of the KLA whom you visited in prison told you in actual fact that they involuntarily joined the KLA or, rather, that they were forced to enter the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were forced to join the KLA; is that it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you happen to ask them how they were forced to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one man told me that the KLA came to his house, and they told him that the following morning he had to have his suitcase -- a small pack ready because he was going to Albania to be trained as a terrorist, and he refused, and they said, "Well, if you refuse, we will kill you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in the monthly reports of the OSCE for the period from mid-January to mid-February 1999, it is stated that the KLA controlled the Albanian community through the police? It policed it and took reprisal measures towards those who had been accused of collaborating with the Serbs? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably true, yes. As we understand it, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also true that in that report of yours, that same report, that mention was made in Pec of several Albanians who were denoted as being loyal to the Serbs and that they were killed in separate incidents? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly, but if it's in the report, then it will be true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember whether it is true that all the Albanians were killed by bullets, shot in the head, bullet shots in the head?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember in this particular incident how they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you happen to know or did you know at the time how many abducted Serb civilians, members of the army or the Ministry of the Interior, at the beginning of 1999, were in the hands of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we had different numbers. I think at one point I heard numbers of greater than 20. The Albanians denied ever having such large numbers of police in captivity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many did your mission succeed in freeing of those individuals, apart from the several soldiers that we mentioned earlier on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that several days ago, in Kosovo, at different locations mass graves were found of Serb victims and that their identification -- the process of their identification is underway? Have you heard about that? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the village of Dragobilje?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I'm not aware of having been in this visit -- in this village. The name doesn't jump out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's where the KLA headquarters were, and that's also where a forward point of the Kosovo Verification Mission was, as well as a forward post of KDOM for links and liaison with the KLA headquarters. I assume that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is what you assert. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the reasons why I would not know anything about this is because I was the liaison officer with the -- to the Serbian commission, and therefore this type of information would have actually been kept from me in case I accidentally gave it away, or I got tempted to go there, or whatever. So I did not go anywhere near this village, or know that the headquarters was there, or what presence there was from the OSCE, or what KDOM did there. And I presume that Mr. Milosevic is referring to the US-KDOM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't help as to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you happen to know -- that is to say, you mentioned yesterday on one occasion with respect to Ramush Haradinaj, their chief, in connection to that, do you know of his statement after the war when he said that meetings with the KVM were mutually significant in view of preparations for the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I'll skip the next few questions, because quite obviously you don't know that. And do you happen to know his opinion and the opinion of other chiefs, KLA chiefs, that they were practically saved with the arrival of your mission and that the presence of your mission enabled them to revive themselves, to become revitalised?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only comment I ever heard them making was that obviously the KVM allowed them to feel safer in Kosovo, and they did talk about that their eventual aim was to achieve -- that what they were trying to achieve was even greater stability in the country by having a Western force, a NATO force, a UN force actually coming -- an armed force coming into Kosovo in order to keep the peace. These were the type of comments that were being made shortly after our arrival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know about or did you discuss in your mission at all the links and connections between the KLA in Kosovo and the Al Qaeda of Osama bin Laden?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that in November 2001 - and this is information that was published in the Wall Street Journal - that there was talk of the presence in Kosovo and in Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We seem to be getting well away from the witness's evidence. Deal with the matters which he gave evidence about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will ask him -- I will deal with the matters which he talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the agreement on the establishment of a mission stresses in principle the KVM's positions and option for cooperation and verification and a respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia -- I assume you know that. That's right, isn't it? That is what it says. On the other hand, I'm sure you know what the goals of the KLA terrorist organisation were, directed precisely against what was contained in your agreement with the Yugoslav government. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know that they didn't sign the agreement, and they were not party to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you cooperated with that side, with that party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been round and round this point, Mr. Milosevic, about the KVM and any relations they may have had with the KLA, and it's not going to assist us to go into it yet again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So within all these restrictions and limitations, I shall try on abridge what I have here as far as possible. You know that against the detained KLA members, legal proceedings, court proceedings were undertaken. I'm sure you know that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that in the report of the OSCE, it is stated, it is also the mid-January, mid-February report 1999, they say that the verifiers of the -- for human rights notice that the recent trials in the district court in Pristina and Pec were conducted in conformity with international standards on legal procedure and that no violation of human rights was noted in these proceedings. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that report, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know about the report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is your own report, January, February. So if it is not correct, then what I'm asking you isn't important. But as it is correct, or let us assume that it is correct without any responsibility on your part for saying that, why did Keller do this in relation to the KLA when legal proceedings were being conducted against them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what did Keller do?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said -- Keller is not important here, but the Verification Mission and its leaders - and Keller was a function of this - why did he insist that members of the KLA be released when legal court proceedings were being undertaken against them? Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's quite simple: There was an agreement made when we released the nine Serbian prisoners that the 11 Albanian prisoners would be released at some date subsequent, not too close to try to link the two, because we didn't -- the Serbian side, this was your insistence, of your people, we didn't want this to appear to look as if it was a we-will-release-them-if-you-release-ours, but that is in fact exactly what it was. It was a quid pro quo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about this principle quid pro quo? How is it being applied now when persons who are terrorists who are serving prison sentences in Serbian are being pardoned and released?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You attended the funeral in Racak?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not actually in the village of Racak. I was not far away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The KVM provided for additional patrols for this particular event. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that, during the funeral, the KLA arrested between 40 and 60 Albanians because, as they had said, they were known as unfit for cooperation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in the OSCE report for the period of January and February, it is mentioned that, during the funeral in Racak, the KLA arrested Albanians with whom they did not have cooperation, and later on, members of the KVM were setting them free. In all fairness, it is not said whether they managed to release all of them, but do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know about it is that your forces arrested a number of suspects in and around the Racak area during the funeral. And I know nothing about the OSCE releasing -- I can't imagine why we would be releasing because the OSCE did not actually hold anybody. We had no facilities to hold anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe the interpretation was not right. The point was, in your report it says that the KLA was arresting Albanians and that the KVM made an effort to have them released. It's not that the KVM was arresting these Albanians. That's what I talked about. And I asked you whether you knew anything about that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many reports of yours during the mission were sent further on to NATO?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of any of our reports being sent to NATO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your assertion that you did not exchange information with NATO and that you did not sent information to NATO from the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not my assertion at all. You asked me if we sent reports to NATO. I was not aware of any reports being sent. However, at one stage during the Rambouillet talks, when we thought that NATO would be the force coming into Kosovo, we did in fact have contact with NATO and we sort of briefed them as to what they could expect when they arrived in Kosovo - where they could be located, the types of roads, et cetera - which would allow the force to move in quickly and easily into Kosovo, as a result of Rambouillet talks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you were involved in armaments and technical equipment, can you say anything about the following: Is it correct that the members of the KVM, after going from Kosovo to Macedonia, maintained contacts with the KLA by way of satellite telephones and other means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe a number of Albanians who were there and maybe asked some of our interpreters, did try to establish communications by satellite telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was even established and even the press in the West wrote about this, that they had direct contacts, by way of these telephones, with the officials of NATO and even directly with General Clark. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that probably is untrue because one of my jobs when I arrived in Macedonia and in Skopje, after a number of weeks, I was seconded -- I was not seconded, I was made the liaison officer to NATO, between NATO and OSCE. And of course, there were other liaison officers there from the UNHCR and other NGOs. So I was one of many who attended some of the briefings, but I never -- never, in all of my time that I visited the NATO headquarters, I never heard anyone say anything about NATO having direct contact with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the mission, did you have positioning devices, equipment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean did we have global positioning systems? Yes, so that we knew where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you only establish where you were or did you also establish the positions of certain points of interest in terms of the ensuing NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- we obviously had maps of the whole of Kosovo, so we would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not need to establish any positions of anything on the ground. We were interested to know where we were and where the -- the VJ, MUP, and KLA were on the ground so that we could make accurate assessments of what was happening in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you explain the fact that the largest number of facilities that were at any point visited by the verifiers was very precisely hit during the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the witness, I don't think. It depends upon the basis of the assertion. Can you help, Colonel, as to whether there's any truth in that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't because I wasn't involved in any of this targeting and the bombing. I was merely sort of sitting in Macedonia as a -- as an observer. But if the targets were barracks, then obviously, you know, everyone knew where these barracks were. We had an agreement with your government that overflight by various types of aircraft had been agreed, and therefore we knew -- everyone knew the location. Especially NATO, these were NATO aircraft that were flying over Kosovo, with your permission. So they would have known where the barracks were, and these are the targets, and yes, you know, the two coincided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about barracks, I'm talking about other facilities and buildings, but I have yet another question. You returned to Kosovo as a NATO officer. How many of your colleagues also returned in that capacity, now in the capacity of NATO officer? How many of your colleagues from the Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first two days, it was just General DZ and myself, and then after I was there for a few weeks, I didn't see any other colleagues, British colleagues, and I can't remember seeing any of the colleagues from the OSCE there. It's possible that later, as a part of a natural roulement, units would have had personnel within them who had previously served in Kosovo with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the time which we've allotted you is now up. If you've got one more question, you can ask it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's difficult for me to make a selection because I have many questions left, but I'm going to put the next one that I had here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about a particular KLA building. You said that this was their hospital. And you said that Serb officers told you that this was a legitimate target. How do you assume that they could have known that this was a hospital when it was clear that the KLA were there and that nobody had marked this as a hospital and that nobody had informed the other party thereof?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The evidence was not that it was a hospital, if it's the same one, but that it was somewhere where the KLA received medical assistance. The point is made it wasn't marked in any way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: However, it was known because the Serbian positions overlooked this building, and they would have seen wounded personnel being taken in and out of it on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I think you said it was the doctor's house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was known as the area doctor's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Wladimiroff, have the amici any questions? Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ciaglinski, what you said earlier on in relation to the information that you have provided to us, the information you received from the person you mentioned, in your previous statement, you explained this, and it is recorded on page 6, the last paragraph of the English version. This is the unredacted version. We did not have this statement of yours until a couple of days ago, and I would like to ask you, before I put any questions to you, to read these two paragraphs in which you refer to this, because everything you said to us here -- I mean, what you said then is correct except for one single thing, that at that time you did not say at all that you had received any kind of information from that person with regard to expulsions. Can you explain why you did not say that in your previous statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The -- when I discussed -- when I wrote this statement, this was something I had actually discussed with the statement-takers, and even giving the information I gave, I put a caveat at the end about this information and its confidentiality and the reasons for it. Because this man, who he is, I thought if I kept to the purely -- the facts as they were given there, the military facts, without elaborating any further, that would be sufficient without, if you like, getting him even further in the mire. I had a good relationship with this person, and the last thing I wanted to do was to damage him or destroy him or put him in danger. And I knew that I would have enough trouble trying to explain or to verify, to give some credence to this anyway, because it was a statement made to me in front of just my interpreter. And so basically I felt that was enough information and the second part wasn't required although I had discussed it. And as I said, I didn't want to incriminate him any further. Probably a stupid loyalty towards this man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the previous list of witnesses provided by the Prosecution, you were supposed to be questioned on the 18th. Mr. Slobodan Milosevic got sick. You were here in the Tribunal. You were at the Office of the Prosecutor. You talked to the Prosecutor. And after this talk we got a certain summary. Even then you did not mention any expulsions. Is that correct? Even then you did not say what you stated yesterday to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, because I felt that all that, that entire section was being deleted. There was no point to embellish it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But also now, when you were here during these past few days, only after these first conversations with you we ultimately got this summary, at first again you did not speak about this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that -- or rather, you gave an explanation, and I don't want to go back to that. But these maps that you got, were they used for offensive combat operations and for NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The maps were passed to NATO at the time of Rambouillet, which would have facilitated their entry and deployment around Kosovo. How they were used later, I have no idea. I did not have access to beyond a certain limit within the NATO headquarters in Skopje, and therefore I do not know what maps they were using.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But therefore, I'm kindly asking you, Mr. Ciaglinski, to look at

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: where you said then that you were supplied by maps, 1.000 to 1.000, that were later used in NATO offensives in regard to certain positions. You said that they were precisely used for that purpose. That's what you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me if these maps were used for bombing. I do not know if they were used for that. But when I entered Kosovo as a NATO officer, I had these maps. So yes, we used these maps. We had these maps for the entry into Kosovo. But I have no idea if they were used for bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, I worked with my assistant, who is also an attorney, and perhaps we made a mistake in the translation, but I think we didn't because we paid particular attention to this. It says here that you said that after that, the maps were used in NATO offensives. These are your words. If I mistranslated them, then I do give up on this.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not privy to the operations as they were taking place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, do you have your witness statement with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes I do, sir. It says: "Utilized in NATO offensive."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you clarify your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By "offensive" I meant here that we -- because it was referred to as an invasion. Therefore, the invasion of Kosovo. The entry into Kosovo to me is the offensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That is your explanation. I do not insist. Could you please just tell me another thing in connection with this? You said today, in response to Mr. Milosevic's questions, that you informed General DZ thereof.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About the expulsions and these other things.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this before you withdrew, as soon as you got this information and this map? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- I was given this information. I then passed it to DZ who chose not to believe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give this to him before you withdrew from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just interested in another thing, Mr. Ciaglinski, in relation to your statement. This is page 9, paragraph 4 of the English version of your statement. Yesterday when you spoke about this event, when the behaviour of the army was perfectly correct, you said that an officer had been wounded. And before that, you said that then when the army was very correct, that a colonel had been killed on that occasion. That is what it says in your statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a colonel was shot. I'm sure I didn't say he was killed. I don't recall anybody being killed during the operation at Labenda -- at Lebane. I think there's often a difference between shot and killed in the translation. "Shot" means not killed, just wounded. But we don't say the person was wounded, we say the person was shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not an expert in that. I got a Serbian translation from the OTP of your statement, and in the Serbian version provided by them, it says that this person was killed. But if this is your explanation, I'm not going to insist. You also refer to the action that you prevented with your activity, and you said that you invested great efforts in order to avoid a conflict because, near that village, there were between 1.000 and 2.000 members of the KLA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, in connection with that, whether as a peace mission you ever tried to find out what the total number of the KLA was. Near that village, there were 1.000 or 2.000 members of the KLA. Did you ever manage to find out, in terms of the information that you were collecting, because that is what you were there for, inter alia, did you ever manage to find out how many of the KLA there were anyway? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very difficult, almost impossible task, because in the first place, we didn't even know who many of the leaders were and who was even in charge of the whole operation. And therefore, I think at the height, you know, just shortly before we left, we could only estimate that there were possibly as many as 10.000 people in some sort of uniform in this organisation loosely known as the KLA. But on this occasion, we actually saw very large numbers of people being brought in from many areas with tractors, with horse-drawn, mule-drawn carts, carrying ammunition and weapons. So this is why we knew what was coming in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you have any approximate knowledge, at least, of the quantity of weapons they had, not only the type of weapons? Did you or did you not have this kind of knowledge? Just give me an answer to that effect.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- whenever we saw a new type of weapon that the KLA had acquired, we would note it, so we knew the new type of weapons coming in, and we roughly knew how many, that they all had a rifle, for example. We tried to guesstimate the number of mortars or rocket-propelled grenades, but they were just estimates and there was no way of actually carrying out an accurate assessment of what they had and how many weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in another area now. You said that you visited this group of Albanians that were supposed to be exchanged for Serb prisoners, and you said everything that you said, I don't have to repeat all of that now. Do you know what they said to you? At that moment when they were in that convoy that was ambushed and shot at, were they wearing civilian clothes then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that as they were crossing the mountains in winter, they would have been wearing a great number of clothes. I know that having seen some of the other photographs taken by -- both our verifiers and the VJ and the MUP, that some of them were wearing uniforms, yes. I mean, there is no dispute that they were carrying weapons and arms across from Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what you said, you said that underneath their uniforms, they perhaps had an extra pair of trousers or something. How much clothing did they actually have? Because they were going through the mountains. You said, when you were describing what was seen, that all of this was double clothing.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a lot of clothes on. I mean, I was not there, I did not examine the bodies; I can only report on things that I read, heard, and saw the photographs. But I believe that they did wear several layers of clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are talking about those who had lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we didn't see the other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you see them? Because you visited them in prison, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time any of us saw them, because we were only shown the bodies at the time, up in the mountains north of Prizren, and the first time we then saw them later was when I went in. I was allowed to go and see them with my interpreter, when they were wearing the clothes that they had to wear in the prison. And these were their own clothing. Some of them were civilian clothing and some of them were combat-type uniforms. And these were the clothes that they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, I have to ask you something. You used a word "village militia" awhile ago. When you were working there, did you realise that in Serb villages and in Albanian villages, there were people who were wearing civilian clothes and yet carrying weapons? Albanians were defending their houses and Serbs were defending their houses. Were there people who carried weapons who were not in the KLA, who were not in the military, who were not in the police and nevertheless they carried weapons and they were defending their homes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. It's -- Kosovo was an area where virtually every householder has a weapon and virtually everybody has a gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's time for the adjournment. Are you going to be many more minutes, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would need about 15 minutes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have decided to cut down my questions, and I shall just be asking something with respect to three documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My first question is as follows, and in fact, my questions refer to Exhibit 94 and tab 63, to be more specific. And it has to do with the chronology of the most important events from the 15th of October to the 18th of April, 1999. You, Mr. Ciaglinski, said yesterday that you knew about that chronology. Somebody asked you about it. Now, I am interested in the following: My first question relates to the 25th of February. Could you take a look at that date, the 25th of February. The number is 110. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says there that it was -- a change was noted in the leadership of the KLA on one side, and immediately after that it says, "The return of the KLA leadership to Kosovo, in the French C130." Now, what is C130? Can you explain to us what you learnt about the changes in KLA leadership? And how come what it says here, that the leadership in Kosovo was returned in a French C130? What is it? Is it a vehicle? Could you explain that to us? What is a French C130?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. A C130 or Charlie 130 is an American built -- designed transport helicopter which transports troops or vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that that American helicopter was used --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you. But never mind. It was an American flyer. Now, do you know who the new leadership was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's make sure we're not at cross-purposes here. As I understand it, it's an American-built aircraft. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And when it says a French C130, it's referring to whichever air force or whatever force it was, that it was responsible for transporting the people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The French took it upon themselves to -- because it was in Rambouillet, they provided the air transport between Kosovo and France and back again, and this is why it was a French owned aircraft but American designed and built.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says something quite different here. First of all, you noted, and this is something that General DZ mentioned yesterday, he referred to the change in leadership and that the leadership was more rigorous and rigid than the previous one. And here note is made of what General DZ precisely said, and it says the leadership was changed, and this changed leadership arrived in Kosovo in that particular aircraft. Is that what happened or did it happen in some other way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we say that the leadership had changed, as a result of the chemistry and discussions in Rambouillet, certain people -- the same people who left are the same people that came back. It's just that their responsibilities within the group emerged differently. So different members of that group took on greater responsibilities and the others were, as a result of the talks, were pushed back into the background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we're not understanding each other. It says here that those people were brought in from Albania. Where were they brought in from? Where did they come to Kosovo from? Where were they brought in from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came back from Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ah, from Rambouillet. But this changed leadership, when did that take place, this change of leadership?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the people that flew out to Rambouillet were exactly the same that came back, so that the KLA leadership that went out came back. It's just that within the group certain individuals emerged as new leaders within that group and others who had previously been leaders of that group had dropped into the background. So there was, if you like, a realignment, a reassessment, their own reassessment as to who really had the greatest voice and the greatest authority within this group of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ah. That makes it clearer. Now with respect to this document, another point I'm interested in, point 121, the 9th of March. According to this chronology it says, and could you explain that, the worry that the KLA was losing control. Who was worried that the leadership of the KLA was losing control over the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, I know that the concern was both within the KLA leadership and also within the OSCE, because we had -- we believed by talking to the KLA leadership we could actually have some influence and some moderating influence on what they were doing. But the local zone commanders, who were not necessarily part of this leadership, were beginning to operate -- some of them were beginning to operate without any reference back to the leadership itself, to the main leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 94, tab 53, is the next one that I would like to look at. Do you know about this assessment of KLA views on the 15th of March?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last page, under "C", the abducted member of the Albanian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. police force, could you read that part, please? "Recognised, acknowledged that the security service of the KLA arrested a member of the Albanian police and that it was holding it in custody in its information centre. That is the first time that the KLA has recognised that it has a police unit, which is effecting that type of operation throughout the region." Now, you had this information, did you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they had a police force, a security unit? Which information?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All -- everything it says under C.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everything you were able to establish via your liaison officer in fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't wish to dwell on D and E, those sections. That relates to cease-fire. But I would like to move on to point 7. I don't want to read it all but it says that under certain conditions and circumstances, the KLA would probably attempt to transfer the fighting to the towns. So you had information of this kind, that unless certain conditions were met, the KLA would try to have the -- to take the fight into the towns and cities. Is that another piece of information that you disposed of, that you had?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now the third document, which is not contained in Exhibit 94, but I have received it and it has to do with your own headquarters. I have it in English here. We needn't -- don't have to look for it. We can show it to Mr. Ciaglinski in English, and I will finish there. Would you have a look at the document, please, sir, and then I will have a question to ask you about it. I have the English version, and it is a Prosecution document 03045428. This is the English version. I do apologise. I've given you the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, once again, is a report by the liaison officer of the KVM headquarters, and under 10, it says that a commander stated: "That if the peace agreement was signed, he would take his units to the hills and carry on guerilla warfare there. And the conclusion is that regardless of what will happen at the next round of peace talks, there is a definite willingness on behalf of members of the KLA to continue fighting." That is the report which your liaison officer wrote. Did you have knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, you said under paragraph 10, did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "B". It was point -- no. The conclusion was under 3. Conclusion, number 3. And it was signed by the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was Chris Lucas's assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is something that you received at the headquarters. I think you were aware of this.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Chris Lucas was a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a couple of questions in re-examination, if I may. Re-examined by Mr. Ryneveld:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday in cross-examination and it was touch upon again sort of obliquely today by the accused, there is a discussion concerning correspondence with Donna Phelan under the signature, if I remember correctly, of the head of the OSCE mission. Actually, I'll read from the transcript, if I may. The question was: "The method that was initially planned by Donna Phelan," and your response was, "She was an experienced weapons -- CFE weapons inspector verifier sitting in the world of verification, et cetera." And you said, "Now, because we chose -- we sort of chose this method and also at the same time Donna Phelan and DZ had written a letter to Mr. Milosevic outlining how we'd like to do this and had no response. She assumes no response means that we had either no option at that point but to carry on with the method we thought of. When this method didn't work that's when we changed it almost immediately. Mr. Milosevic believes that we continued this way. We did not continue the confrontational technique, we went away from that." Now, there's a further dialogue, and Mr. Milosevic said he was not aware of having received letters from Donna Phelan from your verifiers, any one of your verifiers, I have to say that." Your response was, "Yes. First of all, the letter was drafted by Donna Phelan, and given -- signed by the head of mission. That was sent to you." Now, that's the context about which I'm going to -- I'm going to ask you to look at a document, a letter which appears to have the date of the 23rd of November, 1998, addressed to his excellency Mr. Slobodan Milosevic as President of the Republic of Yugoslavia. About three pages, signed by Ambassador William G. Walker, with some attachments. I'd like you to look at that letter, if you would please. It's being distributed now. And ask the Court -- and I would ask you to review that letter and first of all, tell us if that is a letter to which you referred.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 99.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll give you a moment to have a look at the letter with attachments. Witness, I see you've had an opportunity to have a brief cursory glance at the letter. Is that indeed the letter to which you referred in response to questions by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does this letter contain, to the -- from what you can see, the areas that you were attempting to refer to yesterday that went to Mr. Milosevic which he said he didn't see?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further, in the -- I'll get back to that letter in a moment. The cross-examination continued at -- just for the record, I'm reading from the page 3250 of the transcript, Your Honours, and 3251. After the portion that I simply read, Mr. Milosevic said, "I'm not aware of having received -- of having receiving the letters from Donna Phelan from your verifiers, any one of your verifiers, I have to say that. But in relation to this, what you've just described that you found in terms of the verification of the MUP, that is to say your teams did, did you send a report on this to the Yugoslav authorities or, rather, did you discuss this with the Yugoslav commission that was headed by General Loncar in Pristina? "A. Yes. First of all, the letter was drafted by Donna Phelan and given and signed by the Head of Mission. That was sent to you. And secondly, the letter was, the full report of the findings --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies to the translators. I'm reading and then I'm speeding up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The full report of our findings of the 27 positions that were more was passed to General Loncar of the Cooperation Commission, the full report. "Q. And did you discuss this question with General Loncar and his associates? "A. Absolutely. DZ personally discussed it with General Loncar. "Q. So did you discuss it fully with General Loncar? When I say 'you,' I'm not referring to you personally. I'm referring to you the Verification Mission, the appropriate representative, that is." And I'm going to skip over. You said: "It was discussed with the Cooperation Commission and General Loncar, yes." Now, the second document I'd like to show you is a document that appears to be -- it's a draft translation of a document from the Federal Foreign Ministry office in Pristina, dated the 20th of December, 1989, it says, however it's clear from the context that it's 20th of December, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Clerk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, I would like to draw your attention, if I may, to the paragraph numbered 1, where it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that now, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "At the initiative for the KVM for Kosovo and Metohija, General Drewienkiewicz and his associates request to meet urgently with General D. Loncar. In the presence of other members of the coordination team for Kosovo and Metohija, he brought up the problem of verification in the Podujevo region on the basis of our interests that the KVM intensify its patrols in this region to determine the actual state of affairs, something which our side had requested at several of the most recent meetings and discussions conducted by Vice-Premier N. Sainovic with the head of the KVM and by General Loncar at which General Drewienkiewicz was always present." I pause here to say it appears that the letter should be dated 1998, not 1989. It's just obviously a reversal of numbers. "General Drewienkiewicz said that per our request, they had intensified patrols in the Podujevo region and that, to their surprise, they established the presence of Yugoslav army units has been increased lately in an inappropriate manner given the current situation," et cetera, et cetera. Is this document the confirmation by the FRY authorities of the conversation that you related to in your discussions with Mr. Milosevic on this issue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final document I'm going to ask you to refer to, tab 3 of Exhibit 94, which we looked at yesterday, but in context of both the letter Exhibit 99 and the FRY authority's acknowledgment of notification. Tab 3, when you have it, consists of, first of all, what appears to be a record of meeting in Belgrade of the 25th of October, 1998, with a number of signatures. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But then there is a statement attached to that, and looking at the second full paragraph of the statement following the signing page, and I think there's a number 3 written in the bottom right-hand corner, the second full paragraph says: "In order to further encourage the return to peace and normality, the state authorities of the FRY will bring down the level of presence and the equipment of security forces, MUP and VJ, throughout Kosmet to normal levels, i.e., to the levels preceding the outbreak of terrorist activities," et cetera. It then goes on at the -- in the next portions of that agreement, statement, that they have announced -- "The state authorities of the FRY have announced the following measures," and they are enumerated on the next page. And paragraph 8 on page 4: "In order to ensure verification of these provisions, VJ and MUP commanders will provide to KDOM/OSCE detailed weekly reports of manning, weapons, and activities of their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. forces, and will provide immediate notification to KDOM/OSCE of any deployments contrary to these provisions and will explain the circumstances regarding such deployments." Is that the agreement which was attempted to be addressed in the letter signed by Walker to the attention of the then-president of the Republic of Yugoslavia, the accused?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One further question, if I may, in relation to that. The information that is requested in the 23rd November 1998 letter, Exhibit 99 in these proceedings, would the KVM be able to carry out the mission without receiving the requested information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as -- no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are my questions, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I was able to understand, the other party is trying to explain -- the opposite party is trying to explain some of the contradictions and referring to the issues that I raised and that I asked questions about. They are showing William Walker's letter addressed to me, and that is highly probable. And I was just surprised by the fact that Donna Phelan wrote to me, because I'd never heard of Donna Phelan up until this testimony, the testimony of this witness. And the letter shows precisely that there is no letter from Donna Phelan addressed to me. That is letter by the Head of Mission, William Walker. Therefore, that is completely uncontested. There is no letter from anybody else that I received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have the point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the aspects of that assertion -- yes, I do assume that there is nothing that is challenged there. Secondly, look at the contents of the letter.
