It says: "Dear Mr. President, We are ready to start the operations to --" [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... Yugoslavia and OSCE." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. [In English] "FRY provides certain specific information to KVM concerning security forces in Kosovo." [Interpretation] And then we come to the definitions, the definitions which are quite customary and usual: What heavy armaments mean - over 12.7 millimetres - what checkpoints are in respect to personnel and vehicles; what is meant by observation points - that they should not have more than -- not be manned by more than 30 people; and what company-sized teams are - they are the units that are the size of a company. That, too, is nothing that was contested. And as far as I was able to -- I understand, what he writes in the letter, and it's quite clear, anybody with elementary school would be able to understand it, all he's asking for is that these notions be defined in this way, and he seeks detailed information about all the forces in Kosovo and what should be brought in. And when we go through all this, that is up to the 21st in the month, that they expect to have these -- this information, as of the 16th of the month. And then he says in the middle of the second page: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... specific cooperation guidelines for KVM members including procedures for inspection of security forces. Once completed, we will inform you of these guidelines to ensure there is no confusion among FRY Serbian security forces concerning inspections to be executed by KVM verifiers." [Interpretation] So he is speaking about the fact that, in expressing the mission's readiness to start work, he is saying that they are going to define, and precisely define, specific operational instructions, guidelines, methods and so on and that's what his explanation refers to. Now, my question was linked to these methods and referred to the witness statement, to the effect that Donna Phelan developed a method of confrontation, confrontational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, is there some point or question that you want to ask the witness? Because otherwise he's being detained unnecessarily. If there is, you can put it to us and we'll see. Re-cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. My question is as follows: From this letter of Walker's, which refers to very normal work prior to the start of the OSCE commission and information that it is going to develop methods and guidelines, are we able to conclude that some sort of method of confrontation would be developed? That is the question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no method of confrontation developed as such but the method that was developed was because of the reaction of the Serbian units being inspected resulted in confrontation, and that's why we changed it. The letter also was not answered. The letter -- we did not receive the information about your troop sizes, the weapons held, the three points you mention at the front. None of those are in fact -- were complied with. The company group, I think it says 30 people. You breached that. The number of tanks and weapons you had at all these positions were greater, and so on. So I don't think any of those things were really complied with anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you know very well, and you said a moment ago during your testimony that you were -- did have freedom of movement, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to let you argue this over again. We've allowed you to ask the question because you haven't seen the document before. Now, it's time the witness was allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there's the other document that was shown which speaks about the good cooperation, as far as I'm able to see, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have it. We will be able to read it. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ciaglinski. I have a couple of questions. The first simple one is that it's about the information you heard from a high official concerning the proposed manoeuvre. You said that you reported it to General DZ, and you just said -- also said that he chose not to believe it. Is that the reason why that was not put into writing? I noticed everything -- what's happening was put into writing in detail. Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, exactly. It sounded so unbelievable that I think -- I know that DZ -- I discussed it with him, and he said, "Well, you know, this is just possibly one man's opinion." I tried to argue it as such that it was too detailed, but at the time there were so many other things happening, I think he just put it to one side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was there any person you mentioned about --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I discussed this with many people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Then my next question is about the Racak incident. Were you involved in the making of the decision to pull out the KVM people from the investigation site when Judge Marinkovic decided to enter the village with armed policemen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. DZ was there, and as soon as Judge Marinkovic said what she said, DZ looked at me, I left the room. From the balcony outside the police station, I got on the radio for a better signal and immediately I instructed General Maisonneuve to withdraw the troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I can't quite understand is this: You said that your mission had negotiated with the KLA that they would not have armed men in the area. That being the case, why did it necessarily follow that if Judge Marinkovic were to be accompanied by the MUP, it would undoubtedly provoke a gunfight?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because although the KLA gunmen were not in the village, they weren't that far away, as were the MUP forces. They were sitting on one side of the hill, overlooking the village from one side, and the KLA were sitting out of the village on the other side. So it -- as soon as one lot entered, the other lot would enter as well. It was guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that KVM had already got a promise from KLA that there would be no armed men, might not one think that if the KVM mission at that time had not quit the place and instead accompanied the investigating judge, there might have been no gunfights?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the condition -- the only condition the KLA would accept was that if no armed MUP accompanied -- we offered to accompany -- both to flood the village with KVM and also to accompany the judge. She refused us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wasn't it humiliating for a judge to be asked by foreigners, by its KVM mission to be protected -- not to be protected by the police of his or her own country? Did that kind of idea hit upon you at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Presumably what you were concerned about was the risk of what happened; a firefight. If the judge insisted on going in with her own people, you were afraid, as I understand it, that they would be fired upon by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that's precisely what happened.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, thank you for coming. You're free to go. Thank you for giving your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we turn to the 92 bis witnesses, I have just a couple of or two or three broadly procedural matters that I'm wondering if I could just mention them now as there's a change in the type of evidence. None of them will take very long. First, we understand that for reasons that are outside, I think, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any of our control, the Albanian booth will cease to be available from the 10th of May. That's what we've understood. Now, we'll obviously do all we can to use the time between now and then with Albanian-speaking witnesses, but we are concerned that there will be probably some 35 or more witnesses, including 92 bis witnesses, who are likely to be using the Albanian language following that date, and we're also -- and so we're concerned about the effect of the withdrawal of the booth on that part of the case. And we're also more generally concerned about the absence, if there will be an absence, as I assume, of an Albanian language broadcast given the public interest, but that's -- all we can do is express our concerns on that topic if our information is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can take it that the Trial Chamber will also be most concerned about that information is correct. It seems to me it's most important in a trial of this significance that there is proper translation and interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next thing that I have forgotten for a long time but I keep trying to remember to note is this: The Chamber may remember right at the beginning of the trial it asked for Mr. Tapuskovic for a note on the scope of matters historical that he would support as being relevant in this case. We've reminded him of it. It has yet to come, but I have to say that our historical expert evidence is in the process of development, and the sooner that we can have that note the more useful it will be, because it may of course identify issues that aren't immediately in our mind. The next thing is that amongst outstanding issues, there aren't very many, but there's one concerning the 92 bis application for an humanitarian expert witness, and the Chamber may know from the way the application is drafted that there are particular reasons why in a sense it's helpful to have the decision, one way or the other, as early as possible, particularly if as will be the case we would call the witness if the motion is rejected. I'm sorry to not press you on that, but we have procedural difficulties given the particular humanitarian agency concerned. Before I come to the 92 bis witnesses, there's only a couple of other things. We are preparing a further forecast witness list which we'll distribute as soon as we can. We hope it will be as precise as it can be subject to all the unforeseen circumstances. As it looks at the moment, the first municipality evidence, which will be in respect of a killing site and it will be killing site of Racak, should be reached at about mid-May. That's our -- that's our rough estimate. And accordingly, if and -- it's a matter upon which the Chamber has to decide, but if the Chamber is going to build in at all consideration of the safety of evidence about particular municipalities at any advanced stage, our forecast is that Racak, mid-May. And then finally on general issues, I think it was some weeks ago now that I filed the latest Rule 68 position statement where I suggested that we should all, amici, the accused and we ourselves remind ourselves to ask the question has the accused in his cross-examination identified any new topics that require specific consideration for Rule 68 purposes given the approach we're making to Rule 68 purposes. I recall that for our side and at the moment, we haven't yet identified any new parameters, but we remain of course receptive to better ideas that may come from anywhere else in the Court including from the accused, as well as from the amici. Your Honour, can I then turn to the 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you do, I wonder if there's really any point starting a new witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know how long the accused is likely to be in cross-examination of him. Before we come to him, there's probably a few ground rules that will be probably helpful to identify for 92 bis witnesses generally. I've got about three or four points I wanted to raise, but I don't think they'll necessarily be long in disposal, but I'm entirely content to put him back to tomorrow, in which case ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There are one or two matters to deal with. It may be better to start the witness tomorrow than to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, K22 who is going to give evidence in open session, he will then come first, I think, because his timetable constraints are fairly tight, and we'd have the 92 bis witnesses as originally forecast to follow him, but might it be convenient to deal with the 92 bis witness giving issues now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have a ruling in mind on that, which it may be convenient if we deal with. What we have in mind is this: That the -- when the witness is called, we will allow five minutes for an introduction by the Prosecution. So that is merely some introductory questions to allow the witness to become accustomed to giving evidence. His or her statement will, of course, be evidence. We will have read it. We will then allow cross-examination, that being the purpose of our original order. We have in mind the amount of time which has been taken in cross-examination, as I referred to today, a great deal of it in argument, comment, and the like. And in order to restrict that, cross-examination will be limited to one hour unless good cause for continuing beyond that time is allowed. There will then be cross-examination from the amicus and re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much for that. I think that probably covers all the points I was going to raise but about one or two. As to procedural formalities, the witness statements bear the witness's present addresses, and there's no reason for that to be made public. And so we have redacted versions, redacted only as to present addresses. I'm loath to have to burden the Registry and Chamber with two statements of each witness, but it's either got to be in that way because the statement itself will become a public exhibit, or alternatively, and I don't know which is going to be the easier to manage, we could simply serve a redacted statement in all cases with confidentially the sheet of paper that gives the address. Now, I think if I may say so from experience, probably the important thing is to ensure that the procedure is the one that's most convenient to those who have to handle the paperwork, and I express no view other than the interests of the witnesses dictate that their present addresses shouldn't be revealed in a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Follow that course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court will -- I now turn to the question of the five minutes, which was, curiously enough, a figure that had been in my mind as a possibility in any event. However, the question is what is to be covered in the five minutes. The Chamber will recall that on an earlier occasion, I explained how many of these witnesses who were going to be subject to 92 bis, or may have been subject to 92 bis provisions, were concerned that their account should be told, and there's also a concern that there should be a context for the public hearing the evidence, who will only be able to get the full context from exhibited witness statements after the evidence has been given. And accordingly, I will intend, if this is indeed consistent with the ruling that you've just announced, I will intend in the five minutes, and by way of introductory questions, to give the broad structure or, indeed, it will be skeletal structure of what the witness can speak about so that everyone, including the public, may know that this witness is here to speak about X village and what happened in summary to the certain persons and so on. And if that does fit with Your Honours' ruling, then we will prepare the witnesses accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very grateful for that clarification, and we will prepare things accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The one matter which you should deal with is this, obviously; that if there is going to be a problem about the Albanian translation, we obviously need to cover as many Albanian witnesses before that date as possible, even if it means taking them out of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it happens that we were probably going to have a substantially undiluted diet of 92 bis witnesses until the end of April, depending how long the accused takes with them, and that will be followed subject, I think, to one or two witnesses at the most, I haven't re-checked the list, by witnesses as to killing sites who will probably prefer to speak in Albanian in nearly all cases. So I think there was going to be pretty well solid Albanian speakers until the 10th of May in any event. But certainly we will reconsider the matter and possibly postpone any who would not be using the Albanian facilities. There still remains the problem, if it is a problem, of an Albanian language public broadcast in a case which so completely affects the interests of those who speak that language. But I'll probably find out after this that my information is wrong, but this was the information I was provided with yesterday from a couple of sources, and it became a concern to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One matter that I raised to Mr. Ryneveld earlier was that some of the witnesses on the latest list have not yet been the subject of applications, so if you would get those in as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We understand that. We apologise for the oversight. It will be dealt with promptly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what we have heard, that party over there wishes to testify instead of the witnesses, according to your Rule 92 bis. So that means the witness is not going to say what happened to him but Mr. Nice is going to explain what happened to the witness for the purposes and needs of the public, which I think has nothing to do with any manner of testimony that has been seen to date before any courts. So that he cannot testify instead of the witness and explain what happened to the witness instead of the witnesses themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... then the statement will be exhibited so the public, as you call them, can have it. Then you'll be able to cross-examine, which is the crucial point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that then is the problem, because we have here the written statement of an illiterate witness who signs his name with his finger, fingerprint, and then he was not able to read the statement at all, and then that side over there is going to explain briefly what it says in that statement so that the witness does not testify at all. And then it is understood that there will be a sort of possibility for cross-examination of what we haven't heard but just seen in a written statement whom we don't know who wrote it. My second point is this: I asked several times that I be told at least one week in advance the list of witnesses who are going to testify, because as you know, there are a great many of them. The last list, the latest list of witnesses that I received I received in the previous break, and it is quite different from the list of witnesses that was given to me the day before yesterday. The statements of these first witnesses who are to testify Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. tomorrow, according to your 92 bis Rule, that is to say, not to testify but that the Prosecution testify in place of them, I received that a moment ago precisely when this last session was to begin. And they are in Albanian and in English. I asked that the material be given to me and witness statements be given to me in the Serbian language, and at least one week in advance so that -- and that I have a list of witnesses at least a week in advance. I received a list of witnesses one hour ago, and the statements of these first witnesses are in English and Albanian or, rather, Albanian and English, and I received those half an hour ago. I saw them for the first time then, so I'll leave you to draw the conclusions. I think that with procedure of this kind, this false indictment, together with the witnesses, is a shipwreck and you are dealing in manipulations which don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will hear no more comments of that sort. Now, let us get this straight. The first matter is that one witness, the witness to give evidence tomorrow, as I understand it, is in fact going to be K22. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And how long do you anticipate he's going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At least a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So we're not talking about tomorrow's witnesses. Now, the next complaint is that the list has been changed substantially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incorrect. But just dealing with things in order, the accused has had all these statements not only once but twice from us. Earlier, we provided them as a matter of convenience for him on a rolling basis because he will not look at the material he's had. He will have had the 92 bis application which covers these statements. He's had a letter giving the witness order on the 11th of April and the new letter is simply a revision and I'm not sure exactly of the number of changes of that letter. So there it is. So he's not taken by surprise. Can I deal with the particular problem that he identified in relation to the first witness who doesn't have the facility of reading and writing. If that is going to be an issue that the accused wishes to take, I can call the translator/interpreter who has today read the statement over to the witness. It's going to take a little bit more time, but she can come along and explain what she's done so if the accused wishes to assert there's been any interference in the due process of the witness having his or her statement read over, we can cover it, but it will take time, but it will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us wait for the cross-examination. We will adjourn now. Nine o'clock tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We're adjourning now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 1.38 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of April, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
